Abstract

Safety constraints and optimality are important but sometimes conflicting criteria for controllers. Although these criteria are often solved separately with different tools to maintain formal guarantees, it is also common practice in reinforcement learning to simply modify reward functions by penalizing failures, with the penalty treated as a mere heuristic. We rigorously examine the relationship of both safety and optimality to penalties, and formalize sufficient conditions for safe value functions (SVFs): value functions that are both optimal for a given task, and enforce safety constraints. We reveal this structure by examining when rewards preserve viability under optimal control, and show that there always exists a finite penalty that induces a safe value function. This penalty is not unique, but upper-unbounded: larger penalties do not harm optimality. Although it is often not possible to compute the minimum required penalty, we reveal clear structure of how the penalty, rewards, discount factor, and dynamics interact. This insight suggests practical, theory-guided heuristics to design reward functions for control problems where safety is important.

Index Terms: 
Value Functions, Safety, Optimal Control, Strong Duality, Reinforcement Learning, Viability

I Introduction

Value functions concisely represent the global behavior of a dynamical system in a scalar function, and have been well studied in both classical control theory and reinforcement learning (RL). Before solving for the value function, a desired task needs to be accurately translated into a reward function and discount factor. Often, the main challenge of an engineer is to design a reward that approximates the desired task, but is also dense throughout the state space.

Safety often also needs to be encoded, as many tasks implicitly require that a set of failure states is never visited. This is particularly challenging, as there may be states that are not failures themselves, but are still unsafe: all trajectories starting from such states end in failure. This requirement is most naturally written mathematically as a state-space constraint, which can be directly enforced along entire trajectories, such as in model-predictive control [1]. It is less clear how the notion of safety can be directly integrated into value functions through rewards. A common approach is to simply put a large penalty on failing. However, it is still unclear under what conditions this penalty ensures that the resulting value function enforces safety, and when it is a mere heuristic [2, 3]. Furthermore, as adding a penalty is essentially a form of reward shaping, it is unclear whether it affects the optimality of the value function with respect to the original task.

We examine the problem from the perspective of viability theory [4]: a state is in the viability kernel if there exists at least one evolution of the system that never fails. Our core contribution is to examine when rewards preserve viability under optimal control. We frame this as a condition on the value function, thus exposing the structure of safe value function (SVFs): a value function that is both optimal for the original (constrained) task, and avoids failure whenever possible. We then examine how to obtain SVFs by penalizing failure, and show that there always exists a finite penalty that induces an SVF. Furthermore, larger penalties do not lose this property. This insight allows for qualitative predictions on the effects of reward shaping, and provides theory-backed heuristics for designing reward functions when perfect system information is unavailable. We also examine how SVFs relate to existing concepts and practices, such as strong duality. This result is of interest for any approach that employs penalties to discourage constraint violation in dynamical systems.

I-A Related Work

Safety in dynamical systems requires constraints to be enforced along entire trajectories, making path planning and tracking a natural approach [5]. However, this approach is often too computationally demanding to be run online for complex systems. To ease computational burden, constraints are often only enforced on trajectories of finite horizon, such as in sequential trajectory planning [6, 7] and model-predictive control (MPC) [1, 8]. Since these methods only enforce constraints along partial trajectories, guaranteeing safety requires additional conditions to be met. For example, in MPC, it is known that the choice of terminal constraint plays an important role in guaranteeing safety [1, Section 2.2]. To forego this terminal constraint typically requires assumptions of local controllability towards equilibrium [9], [10, Chapter 6], which implies viability, to guarantee feasibility and avoid trivially infinite costs. The latter has also been addressed by introducing discounting [11], but viability is still assumed for feasibility. In contrast, we do not assume viability, but study how costs/rewards can be used to guarantee the whole viability kernel’s invariance under optimal control.

Trajectory evaluations can be sidestepped by constraining the system to remain in a controlled positive invariant set. However, these sets are often difficult to compute in practice. One approach is to formulate safety as an ad-hoc optimal control problem, as studied in Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability analysis [12]. The resulting value function can then be used to enforce safety using a backup controller [13, 14], and is completely agnostic in the task formulation. Another closely related approach is control barrier functions (CBFs) [15, 16], which generalizes the backup controller of HJ reachability with sets of safety-preserving control inputs, which can again be used as task-agnostic backup controllers. This specialized function can be combined with any existing controller to ensure safety. However, designing a valid CBF is very challenging in practice, and still requires solving an often equally challenging task of designing an optimal controller. In this article, we present SVFs as the natural combination of safety and optimality in a single object, and examine the conditions and requirements such that guarantees are not lost. In particular, the guarantees will rely on choosing a high enough penalty, and only require mild assumptions on the system dynamics. Because of this, we expect that SVFs will be amenable to popular reinforcement learning algorithms.

Even when accurate models are available, finding reachable sets or CBFs typically requires extensive system knowledge or computational effort [17, 18]. This has motivated the interest in learning or refining these objects from data [19, 20, 21, 22]. A novel approach aims at opening up the toolbox of reinforcement learning (RL) for the computation of reachable sets [23, 7]. In the usual case where the optimal behavior is also learned from data, however, a competition arises between exploring for safety and for optimality. This creates the need for exploration strategies that balance these two separate objectives [24, 25]. SVFs are immediately relevant to this branch of research, as they are also amenable to standard reinforcement learning methods.

The idea of accounting for failure directly in the control objective is not new [26]. A pragmatic way of doing this is by penalizing failure states. The penalty is then seen as a design choice controlling the risk of optimal controllers [27], or as a parameter that must be optimized over to allow for the least conservative safe behavior [5, 28]. From a theoretical perspective, it is still unclear whether optimal controllers of penalized problems are optimal with respect to the original constrained task [2, 29], or if they even enjoy safety guarantees; recent literature suggest that they only achieve a weak form of safety [3, Section 2.1.3]. From a practical perspective, the penalty choice is treated as a heuristic; nonetheless, controllers obtained with this approach often yield good results [30, 31, 32], and are frequently deployed on real system [33, 34, 35, 36]. Indeed, a recent benchmark [37, Section 5.3] reports that penalty methods find nontrivial, constraint-satisfying controllers on the safety-gym suite, outperforming constrained RL algorithms such as CPO [38]. Our results reconcile this gap between theory and practice. We prove that there always exists a finite penalty, such that the resulting value function is both safe and optimal. Furthermore, larger penalties still enjoy this property.

In practice, policies and value functions are typically parameterized and solved numerically. In such cases, choosing an arbitrarily large penalty may result in poor exploration [39] and/or an ill-conditioned problem. Such numerical issues are well known in penalty methods used in classical constrained optimization [40, Section 5.4]. Algorithms such as augmented Lagrangian methods address this by iteratively adjusting the penalty, such that it remains small yet sufficiently large to converge to within an arbitrary approximation error [39]. For clarity of exposition, we keep the focus of this article on the mathematical objects, and do not tackle the issue of approximation errors, which is an active field of research [28]. It is reasonable to expect that, just as in penalty methods, it is desirable to choose the smallest sufficiently large penalty, even though in theory larger penalties still result in SVFs. The conditions we derive reveal clear structure of how a sufficiently large penalty depends on discounting, properties of the system dynamics, and reward shaping. Although a closed-form solution is often not attainable, this structure nonetheless provides clear intuition for choosing useful penalties in practice.

Optimizing a return under a running-cost constraint is also studied as constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs) [41]. They provide the necessary theory to describe the solutions to problems with bounded-risk constraints. We explain in detail how our problem relates to general CMDPs and, specifically, to their duality properties. It is also known that tools for unconstrained MDPs such as value functions are only marginally useful for the analysis of general CMDPs [41, 42]. These concerns are void for our problem and, in fact, our analysis heavily relies on value functions. Indeed, we show that our problem is essentially an unconstrained MDP in a controlled-invariant set (the viability kernel).

Finally, there is substantial work that aims at iteratively solving the constrained optimal control problem while guaranteeing safety of the (potentially still suboptimal) controller at every iteration [38, 43, 25, 7]. These approaches typically restrict exploration to enforce safety, and often allow for convergence to a safe but suboptimal (with respect to the original problem statement) controller. Our work is of independent interest; we do not focus on learning safely, but on the safety and optimality properties of the optimal controller for the unconstrained problem.

I-B Outline

The article is organized as follows. In Section II, we begin with preliminaries and notations. In Section III, we state the considered problem. In Section IV, we continue with our two main contributions, i) the concept of safe value functions; and ii) how to enforce it with penalties. In Section V, we discuss the connections between SVFs and related approaches such as strong duality in depth. In Section VI, we illustrate the exposed structure in different settings with simple examples, and interpret the structure to suggest practical heuristics for choosing penalties, thresholds, and reward functions. In Section VII, we conclude with a brief summary, discussion, and outlook. Appendix -A contains the proof of our main theorem and Appendix -B illustrates Remark 3 with examples.

II Preliminaries and Notations

This section introduces the necessary mathematical objects to define safety and optimality. In particular, we address dynamical systems, value functions, and viability theory.

II-A Dynamical Systems

Our core contributions holds in both continuous- and discrete-time; unless otherwise stated, we present both results together. For brevity, we consider the time variable tt belonging to the set 𝕋\mathbb{T}, defined as ℝ+\mathbb{R}^{+} or ℕ\mathbb{N} as appropriate. Integrals on 𝕋\mathbb{T} are defined with the Lebesgue measure when 𝕋=ℝ+\mathbb{T}=\mathbb{R}^{+}, and with the counting measure when 𝕋=ℕ\mathbb{T}=\mathbb{N}.

II-A1 Continuous-Time System

In continuous time, we consider the following deterministic dynamical system:

x˙​(t)=f⁡(x⁡(t),u⁡(x⁡(t))),\dot{x}(t)=f(x(t),u(x(t))), (1)

where t∈ℝ+t\in\mathbb{R}^{+} is time, x⁡(t)∈𝒳⊂ℝnx(t)\in\mathcal{X}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} is the state, u⁡(x⁡(t))∈𝒰⊂ℝmu(x(t))\in\mathcal{U}\subset\mathbb{R}^{m} is a control input, and f:𝒳×𝒰→ℝnf:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{U}\to\mathbb{R}^{n} is the dynamics. The function u:𝒳→𝒰u:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{U} is a feedback controller, and is assumed to be measurable. We denote 𝔘\mathfrak{U} the set of measurable feedback controllers. Our results rely heavily on trajectories: we define ϕxu:ℝ+→𝒳\phi_{x}^{u}:\mathbb{R}^{+}\to\mathcal{X} as the trajectory starting in x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} and following the controller u∈𝔘u\in\mathfrak{U}. We assume that trajectories are well-defined and continuous for all time, which can be enforced with appropriate assumptions on ff.

II-A2 Discrete-Time System

In discrete-time, we consider the following deterministic dynamical system:

xt+1=f⁡(xt,u⁡(xt)),x_{t+1}=f(x_{t},u(x_{t})), (2)

where t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N}. The discrete-time setting allows for weaker assumptions, such as non-continuous dynamics ff or finite sets. Our results readily generalize when stochastic controllers are allowed: we mainly describe properties of unconstrained optimal control problems, whose optimal controllers can always be chosen to be deterministic. Stochasticity is not considered here for clarity; we will discuss this more in Remark 5.

II-B Optimality

II-B1 Reward and Return

We assume a measurable and bounded reward function r:𝒳×𝒰→ℝr:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{U}\to\mathbb{R}. For a given controller u∈𝔘u\in\mathfrak{U} and initial state x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, the return GG is:

G⁡(x,u)=∫𝕋e−tτ⋅r⁡(ϕxu​(t),u^x​(t))​𝑑t,G(x,u)=\int_{\mathbb{T}}e^{-\frac{t}{\tau}}\cdot r(\phi_{x}^{u}(t),\hat{u}_{x}(t))\,dt, (3)

where we use the shorthand u^x​(t)=u⁡(ϕxu​(t))\hat{u}_{x}(t)=u(\phi_{x}^{u}(t)), and τ\tau is a positive discount rate. In discrete time, the discount factor γ\gamma is commonly used instead, with:

γ=e−1τ.\gamma=e^{-\frac{1}{\tau}}. (4)

The discount rate quantifies the problem-specific time-horizon: the smaller τ\tau, the less influence rewards far in the future have on G⁡(x,u)G(x,u). Delayed rewards can nonetheless overcome the effects of discounting if they are large: the effective time horizon results from these competing effects. Since the reward is bounded, the return is finite for every u∈𝔘u\in\mathfrak{U} and x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}.

II-B2 Optimal Control and Value Function

We consider the classical setting of Lagrange optimal control and reinforcement learning: given an initial state distribution on 𝒳\mathcal{X}, find a controller that maximizes the expected value of the return (3). Such a controller will be called optimal. If the maximization is subject to some safety constraint, we say that the controller is optimal for the constrained problem.

A natural object for finding and analysing optimal controllers in RL is the (optimal) value function:

v:x∈𝒳↦supu∈𝔘G⁡(x,u).v:~x\in\mathcal{X}\mapsto\sup_{u\in\mathfrak{U}}~G(x,u). (5)

Finding this value function iteratively from data is the goal of a large branch of reinforcement learning [44, Section 3.6]. An important property of vv is that it satisfies the dynamic programming identity for all t∈𝕋t\in\mathbb{T} and x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} [45, Lemma I–4.2]:

v(x)=supu∈𝔘[∫0te−sτ⋅r(ϕxu(s),u^x(s))ds+e−t+δ​tτv(ϕxu(t+δt))],\begin{split}v(x)=\sup_{u\in\mathfrak{U}}&\left[\int_{0}^{t}e^{-\frac{s}{\tau}}\cdot r(\phi_{x}^{u}(s),\hat{u}_{x}(s))ds\right.\\ &\left.+e^{-\frac{t+{\delta t}}{\tau}}v(\phi_{x}^{u}(t+{\delta t}))\vphantom{\int_{0}^{t}}\right],\end{split} (6)

where δ​t{\delta t} is 1 if 𝕋=ℕ\mathbb{T}=\mathbb{N}, and 00 otherwise.

II-C Safety and Viability

We consider safety as a state-space constraint: there is an absorbing, closed failure set 𝒳F⊂𝒳{\mathcal{X}_{F}}\subset\mathcal{X} of states that the system should never visit. Safety is defined as avoiding the failure set.

Failure is challenging to cope with, even though it is often straightforward to define. Indeed, it is insufficient to simply constrain the controller to stay in the complement of the failure set at each step, as this constraint might eventually become infeasible: there may be states that have not failed yet but from which failure can no longer be avoided within finite time. This is addressed through viability theory [4, Chapter 2]:

Definition 1 (Viability kernel).

The viability kernel 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}} is the set of states from where failure can be avoided for all time:

𝒳V={x∈𝒳,∃u∈𝔘,∀t∈𝕋,ϕxu(t)∉𝒳F}.{\mathcal{X}_{V}}=\left\{x\in\mathcal{X},\exists u\in\mathfrak{U},\forall t\in\mathbb{T},\phi_{x}^{u}(t)\notin{\mathcal{X}_{F}}\right\}. (7)

We call its complement the unviability kernel, and denote it as 𝒳U=𝒳∖𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{U}}=\mathcal{X}\setminus{\mathcal{X}_{V}}. Trajectories can stay in 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}} for an arbitrarily long time, but as soon as they leave it, they fail within finite time. The viability kernel is therefore the largest safe set.

Remark 1.

By definition, trajectories starting in 𝒳U{\mathcal{X}_{U}} fail within finite time. We reconcile this with infinite time-horizon by instantly transitioning the system to an invariant sink state when it reaches the failure set. We forego introducing this formally, as it adds notational burden with no practical benefit.

A safe controller can thus be defined as:

Definition 2 (Safe controller).

We say that a controller u∈𝔘u\in\mathfrak{U} is safe for the point x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} if the trajectory ϕxu\phi_{x}^{u} avoids 𝒳F{\mathcal{X}_{F}} for all time:

∀t∈𝕋,ϕxu​(t)∉𝒳F.\forall t\in\mathbb{T},~\phi_{x}^{u}(t)\notin{\mathcal{X}_{F}}. (8)

Additionally, we say that a controller is safe if it is safe for all points x∈𝒳Vx\in{\mathcal{X}_{V}}. We define 𝔘safe​(x)\mathfrak{U}_{\mathrm{safe}}(x) as the set of controllers that are safe for the point x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, and 𝔘safe=⋂x∈𝒳V𝔘safe​(x)\mathfrak{U}_{\mathrm{safe}}=\bigcap_{x\in{\mathcal{X}_{V}}}\mathfrak{U}_{\mathrm{safe}}(x) as the set of safe controllers.

From the definition of 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}}, it is immediately clear that Equation (8) can be replaced with ϕxu​(t)∈𝒳V\phi_{x}^{u}(t)\in{\mathcal{X}_{V}} for all t∈𝕋t\in\mathbb{T}.

We will later formulate a constrained optimization problem over the set of safe controllers, and consider dual relaxations of this problem: we therefore describe 𝔘safe​(x)\mathfrak{U}_{\mathrm{safe}}(x) as a level set.

Lemma 1.

For x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} and u∈𝔘u\in\mathfrak{U}, define the (discounted) risk ρ\rho as:

ρ⁡(x,u)=∫𝕋e−tτ⋅δ𝒳F​(ϕxu​(t))​𝑑t,\rho(x,u)=\int_{\mathbb{T}}e^{-\frac{t}{\tau}}\cdot\delta_{{\mathcal{X}_{F}}}(\phi_{x}^{u}(t))dt, (9)

where δ𝒳F\delta_{{\mathcal{X}_{F}}} is the Dirac distribution in continuous time, or the indicator function in discrete time. A controller u∈𝔘u\in\mathfrak{U} is safe for x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} if, and only if, ρ⁡(x,u)=0\rho(x,u)=0.

Proof:

The lemma follows from the definition of δ𝒳F\delta_{{\mathcal{X}_{F}}}: this integral evaluates to e−tf/τe^{-{t_{f}}/{\tau}}, where tf∈𝕋∪{∞}t_{f}\in\mathbb{T}\cup\{\infty\} is the time-to-failure of uu from xx, infinite if the trajectory never fails. By Definition 2, uu is safe for xx if, and only if, ϕxu​(t)∉𝒳F\phi_{x}^{u}(t)\notin{\mathcal{X}_{F}} for all t∈𝕋t\in\mathbb{T}, i.e., if, and only if, tf=∞t_{f}=\infty. This concludes the proof. ∎

Although the discount term e−t/τe^{-{t}/{\tau}} is not necessary for the lemma to hold, it will be useful later to linearly combine the risk ρ\rho with the return GG.

III Problem Statement: Safety Through Penalization

We consider a standard control or reinforcement learning problem with dynamics ff (cf. Section II-A), failure set 𝒳F{\mathcal{X}_{F}}, viability kernel 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}}, and return GG as defined in (3). Our goal is to find an optimal controller for the safety-constrained problem:

supu∈𝔘safe𝔼x∼μ⁡[G⁡(x,u)],\sup_{u\in\mathfrak{U}_{\mathrm{safe}}}\expected_{x\sim\mu}\left[G(x,u)\right], (𝒞\mathcal{C})

where μ\mu is the initial state probability distribution, whose support is included in 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}}. Since solving constrained optimal control problems is hard in general, a common approach is to relax the constraint u∈𝔘safeu\in\mathfrak{U}_{\mathrm{safe}} and penalize reaching the failure set 𝒳F{\mathcal{X}_{F}}. This is done by replacing the reward rr by r−p⋅δ𝒳Fr-p\cdot\delta_{{\mathcal{X}_{F}}}, where p∈ℝ+p\in\mathbb{R}^{+} is a (constant) penalty chosen by the designer. We call this unconstrained problem the penalized problem, and define its value function as

Vp:x∈𝒳↦supu∈𝔘G⁡(x,u)−p⋅ρ⁡(x,u).V_{p}:x\in\mathcal{X}\mapsto\sup_{u\in\mathfrak{U}}~G(x,u)-p\cdot\rho(x,u). (𝒫\mathcal{P})

We assume that the supremum is attained and refer to solutions as optimal controllers of VpV_{p}. The question we answer is:

Problem 1.

Under what conditions on pp are solutions of the penalized problem also solutions of the constrained problem? In other words, when are the solutions of ( P ) both safe and optimal for ( C )?

IV Main Result

This section presents our main result: any large enough penalty results in safe and optimal controllers. Since the value function induces optimal controllers via the dynamic programming principle, it indirectly encodes the regions of the state space that will be visited, and those that will be avoided. We can thus define safety of optimal controllers as a property of the value function directly; we call such value functions safe. We first combine this observation with viability theory to identify the properties and sufficient conditions for SVFs. We then show in detail how we can leverage penalties to manipulate the value function and enforce safety.

IV-A Safety as a Property of the Value Function

The standard definition of safety is a point-wise statement for a fixed controller (cf. Definition 2). For this definition, the trajectory must be unrolled to check if it ever enters the failure set. We generalize this point-wise definition to a uniform notion of safety over optimal controllers. These controllers are directly induced by the value function; therefore their safety can naturally be stated as a condition on the value function:

Definition 3 (Safe value function).

Consider a value function vv as given in (5). We say that vv is a safe value function if all of its optimal controllers are both safe and optimal with respect to ( C ).

We emphasize that all SVFs are value functions in the classical RL sense.

Proposition 1.

Consider VpV_{p} as given in ( P ). If VpV_{p} is an SVF, then:

Vp​(x)=V⁡(x),∀x∈𝒳V,V_{p}(x)=V(x),~\forall x\in{\mathcal{X}_{V}}, (10)

where VV is the constrained value function:

V:x∈𝒳V↦supu∈𝔘safeG⁡(x,u).V:\,x\in{\mathcal{X}_{V}}\mapsto\sup_{u\in\mathfrak{U}_{\mathrm{safe}}}G(x,u). (11)
Proof:

This directly follows from Definition 3 and the fact that ρ⁡(x,u)=0\rho(x,u)=0 for x∈𝒳Vx\in{\mathcal{X}_{V}} and u∈𝔘safeu\in\mathfrak{U}_{\mathrm{safe}}. Since optimal controllers of VpV_{p} are in 𝔘safe\mathfrak{U}_{\mathrm{safe}}, they also maximize G⁡(x,u)G(x,u) over 𝔘safe\mathfrak{U}_{\mathrm{safe}}, which is the definition of VV. ∎Proposition 11 illustrates how, in an SVF, optimality is decoupled from safety. Crucially, optimal trajectories starting from initial conditions inside the viability kernel 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}} remain viable and, therefore, the values in 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}} are unaffected by the values outside of it; here, Vp|𝒳VV_{p|{\mathcal{X}_{V}}} does not depend on pp if VpV_{p} is an SVF. This prompts the more general observation that, as long as the reward in 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}} is the same as in ( C ), then all SVFs have the same value in 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}}. It follows that modifications of the reward that only affect the value of 𝒳U{\mathcal{X}_{U}} can be used as a degree of freedom to ensure safety, without affecting optimality. This can be difficult to do in practice, as the viability kernel itself is rarely known with accuracy. We will show sufficient conditions for failure penalties to stop affecting values in 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}} and only affect 𝒳U{\mathcal{X}_{U}}, resulting in an SVF. To do so, we first derive a more practical condition to check that a value function is safe.

IV-A1 The Zeroth-Order Condition for Safety

Our key intuition is that, for an optimal controller to be safe, it is sufficient that states outside the viability kernel 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}} are less attractive than states inside 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}}. We first introduce the notations

R𝒬U=sup𝒬Ur,andR𝒬V=inf𝒬Vr,{R}_{{\mathcal{Q}_{U}}}=\sup_{{\mathcal{Q}_{U}}}\,r,\quad\text{and}\quad{R}_{{\mathcal{Q}_{V}}}=\inf_{{\mathcal{Q}_{V}}}\,r,

as well as 𝒬V=f−1​(𝒳V)⊂𝒳V×𝒰{\mathcal{Q}_{V}}=f^{-1}({\mathcal{X}_{V}})\subset{\mathcal{X}_{V}}\times\mathcal{U} and 𝒬U=(𝒳×𝒰)∖𝒬V{\mathcal{Q}_{U}}=(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{U})\setminus{\mathcal{Q}_{V}} for 𝕋=ℕ\mathbb{T}=\mathbb{N}. Intuitively, 𝒬V{\mathcal{Q}_{V}} is the set of state-control pairs that transition into the viability kernel [46].

Theorem 1 (Zeroth-order condition).

Consider VpV_{p} as given in ( P ). Assume that the following zeroth-order condition holds:

sup𝒳UVp\displaystyle\sup_{{\mathcal{X}_{U}}}V_{p}~ <inf𝒳VV,\displaystyle<~\inf_{{\mathcal{X}_{V}}}V, if​𝕋=ℝ+,\displaystyle\text{if}~\mathbb{T}=\mathbb{R}^{+}, (𝒵\mathcal{Z}a)
R𝒬U+γ⋅sup𝒳UVp\displaystyle{R}_{{\mathcal{Q}_{U}}}+\gamma\cdot\sup_{{\mathcal{X}_{U}}}V_{p}~ <R𝒬V+γ⋅inf𝒳VV,\displaystyle<~{R}_{{\mathcal{Q}_{V}}}+\gamma\cdot\inf_{{\mathcal{X}_{V}}}V, if​𝕋=ℕ.\displaystyle\text{if}~\mathbb{T}=\mathbb{N}.\hphantom{{}^{+}} (𝒵\mathcal{Z}b)

Then, the value function VpV_{p} is safe.

Proof:

See Appendix -A. ∎

Condition (11) ensures that an optimal controller never chooses to leave the viability kernel by ensuring that unsafe actions are immediately sub-optimal. The “zeroth-order” terminology comes from the fact that it directly compares the value of VpV_{p} in different states.

IV-B The Penalty Should Be Big Enough

The intuition for penalizing the failure set 𝒳F{\mathcal{X}_{F}} is that it reduces the values along trajectories that end in failure. A natural question is then if this strategy leads to an SVF. We will now show that, under an additional assumption, it does: increasing penalties causes VpV_{p} to decrease arbitrarily and monotonically in 𝒳U{\mathcal{X}_{U}}. From Proposition 11, this also ensures that VpV_{p} converges to VV inside 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}}. It is, therefore, always possible to enforce the zeroth-order condition (11). The following assumption makes the above reasoning hold:

Assumption 1.

The time to failure in 𝒳U{\mathcal{X}_{U}} is uniformly upper-bounded by Tf∈𝕋{T_{f}}\in\mathbb{T}.

The time Tf{T_{f}} bounds the finite time-to-failure in 𝒳U{\mathcal{X}_{U}} given by viability theory. It can be understood as the time-scale of failure for the system of interest.

Lemma 2 (Influence of the penalty).

Under Assumption 1, the following holds:

  1. (i)

    For every x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, the function p↦Vp​(x)p\mapsto V_{p}(x) is nonincreasing;

  2. (ii)

    The value function is uniformly upper bounded on 𝒳U{\mathcal{X}_{U}}:

    sup𝒳UVp\displaystyle\sup_{{\mathcal{X}_{U}}}V_{p}~ ≤R𝒳U​τ​(1−e−Tfτ)−p⋅e−Tfτ,\displaystyle\leq~{R}_{{\mathcal{X}_{U}}}\tau\left(1-e^{-\frac{{T_{f}}}{\tau}}\right)-p\cdot e^{-\frac{{T_{f}}}{\tau}}, if​𝕋=ℝ+,\displaystyle\text{if}~\mathbb{T}=\mathbb{R}^{+}, (12a)
    sup𝒳UVp\displaystyle\sup_{{\mathcal{X}_{U}}}V_{p}~ ≤R𝒳U⋅1−γTf+11−γ−p⋅γTf,\displaystyle\leq~{R}_{{\mathcal{X}_{U}}}\cdot\frac{1-\gamma^{{T_{f}}+1}}{1-\gamma}-p\cdot\gamma^{T_{f}}, if​𝕋=ℕ,\displaystyle\text{if}~\mathbb{T}=\mathbb{N}\hphantom{{}^{+}}, (12b)

    where Tf{T_{f}} is given in Assumption 1, and where we define R𝒳U{R}_{{\mathcal{X}_{U}}} as:

    R𝒳U=sup𝒳U×𝒰r.{R}_{{\mathcal{X}_{U}}}=\sup_{{\mathcal{X}_{U}}\times\mathcal{U}}~r. (13)
Proof:

Statement (i) is an immediate consequence of the fact that the supremum over 𝔘\mathfrak{U} preserves inequalities. We prove 13 by using classic results on the sup\sup function:

Vp​(x)≤supu∈𝔘G⁡(x,u)−p⋅infu∈𝔘ρ⁡(x,u),V_{p}(x)\leq\sup_{u\in\mathfrak{U}}G(x,u)-p\cdot\inf_{u\in\mathfrak{U}}\rho(x,u), (14)

for all x∈𝒳Ux\in{\mathcal{X}_{U}}. The first term of the right-hand side (RHS) of this equation is upper-bounded by:

R𝒳U⋅τ⁡(1−e−Tfτ),{R}_{{\mathcal{X}_{U}}}\cdot\tau\left(1-e^{-\frac{{T_{f}}}{\tau}}\right), (15)

when 𝕋=ℝ+\mathbb{T}=\mathbb{R}^{+}, and:

R𝒳U⋅1−γTf+11−γ,{R}_{{\mathcal{X}_{U}}}\cdot\frac{1-\gamma^{{T_{f}}+1}}{1-\gamma}, (16)

when 𝕋=ℕ\mathbb{T}=\mathbb{N}. Now, we use the fact that the time to failure from x∈𝒳Ux\in{\mathcal{X}_{U}} is upper bounded by Tf{T_{f}} uniformly in u∈𝔘u\in\mathfrak{U} to bound the second term:

ρ⁡(x,u)=∫0Tfe−tτ​δ𝒳F​(ϕxu​(t))​𝑑t≥e−Tfτ.\rho(x,u)=\int_{0}^{T_{f}}e^{-\frac{t}{\tau}}\delta_{{\mathcal{X}_{F}}}(\phi_{x}^{u}(t))dt\geq e^{-\frac{{T_{f}}}{\tau}}. (17)

Since this is valid for all x∈𝒳Ux\in{\mathcal{X}_{U}}, this proves 13. ∎

The main insight we gain from this lemma is in (12): the supremum of VpV_{p} on the unviability kernel can be made arbitrarily low by increasing the penalty. Therefore, there is a threshold penalty above which the value function is safe:

Theorem 2.

Under Assumption 1, there exists p⋆∈ℝ+p^{\star}\in\mathbb{R}^{+} such that, for all p>p⋆p>p^{\star}, the penalized value function VpV_{p} is safe and the zeroth-order condition (11) holds, with:

p⋆=\displaystyle p^{\star}= [R𝒳U⋅τ−inf𝒳VV]⋅eTfτ−R𝒳U⋅τ,\displaystyle\left[{R}_{{\mathcal{X}_{U}}}\cdot\tau-\inf_{{\mathcal{X}_{V}}}V\right]\cdot e^{\frac{{T_{f}}}{\tau}}-{R}_{{\mathcal{X}_{U}}}\cdot\tau,
if​𝕋=ℝ+,\displaystyle\quad\text{if}~\mathbb{T}=\mathbb{R}^{+}, (18a)
p⋆=\displaystyle p^{\star}= [R𝒳U⋅1−γTf+11−γ+R𝒬U−R𝒬Vγ−inf𝒳VV]⋅1γTf,\displaystyle\left[{R}_{{\mathcal{X}_{U}}}\cdot\frac{1-\gamma^{{T_{f}}+1}}{1-\gamma}+\frac{{R}_{{\mathcal{Q}_{U}}}-{R}_{{\mathcal{Q}_{V}}}}{\gamma}-\inf_{{\mathcal{X}_{V}}}V\right]\cdot\frac{1}{\gamma^{{T_{f}}}},
if​𝕋=ℕ.\displaystyle\quad\text{if}~\mathbb{T}=\mathbb{N}\hphantom{{}^{+}}. (18b)
Proof:

This is an immediate consequence of Lemma 2. Indeed, with the value of p⋆p^{\star} given in (18), the upper bound (12) ensures that (11) holds. ∎As the penalty pp increases, the penalized objective Vp​(x)V_{p}(x) decreases. For x∈𝒳Vx\in{\mathcal{X}_{V}}, Vp​(x)V_{p}(x) is lower bounded, and after pp passes p⋆p^{\star} the value coincides with V⁡(x)V(x). For x∉𝒳Vx\notin{\mathcal{X}_{V}}, the value Vp​(x)V_{p}(x) goes to −∞-\infty as pp goes to ∞\infty.

Finally, we can answer Problem 1 and describe how penalized and constrained problems relate to each other. For penalties p>p⋆p>p^{\star}, the two problems are equivalent. In a nutshell, we provide theoretical justification for penalizing failures based on the following arguments:

  1. (i)

    The critical threshold p⋆p^{\star} is finite;

  2. (ii)

    All maximizers of ( P ) for p>p⋆p>p^{\star} are safe;

  3. (iii)

    All maximizers of ( P ) for p>p⋆p>p^{\star} are optimal for the constrained problem ( C );

  4. (iv)

    The critical threshold p⋆p^{\star} explicitly depends on the maximum time to failure, reward function, and discount rate.

In practice, (iv) is critical for scaling the penalty. For example, the ratio Tf/τ{{T_{f}}}/{\tau} measures how the time-scale of failure compares to the agent’s inner time horizon. Due to the exponential dependency, the required penalties can be extremely large if the agent is short-sighted, i.e., τ\tau is much smaller than Tf{T_{f}}.

Remark 2.

Theorem 2 extends to the case where failure is non absorbing by increasing the threshold penalty p⋆p^{\star} accordingly. The key idea is to adapt Equation (12) to account for the additional reward that can be collected after failure, which is bounded due to discounting. For brevity, we leave this derivation to the interested reader.

Remark 3.

The zeroth-order condition (11) is a sufficient condition for a discontinuous value function to be safe, and Assumption 1 is a sufficient condition to enforce this zeroth-order condition. Both require non-Lipschitz dynamics [47, Proposition 3.1].

This is because when the state-control space is continuous and 𝕋=ℝ+\mathbb{T}=\mathbb{R}^{+}, the dynamics determine whether SVFs are continuous or discontinuous. To extend the presented results to models with Lipschitz dynamics, higher-order conditions are needed. Alternatively, one may approximate a Lipschitz model, for example with hybrid dynamics, to account for Assumption 1 and use the zeroth-order condition. Indeed, models with Lipschitz dynamics often make predictions of unbounded time-to-failure that do not match empirical observations, even when they are accurate and useful for control. This mismatch between model predictions and observations lends itself to the common adage “all models are wrong, some are useful” [48]; Lipschitz-continuity is a very useful assumption for control, where we typically wish to stay well within the viability kernel, but the same models are typically not accurate for bounding the time-to-failure. We include in Appendix -B two examples where Assumption 1 is reasonable for a system that is otherwise well-modeled with a Lipschitz dynamics model.

V Connections to Other Approaches for Safe Control

We explicitly connect SVFs to Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability and control barrier functions (CBFs). In particular, we pinpoint their conceptual differences with SVFs despite apparent similarities. Further, we put our results into perspective to well-known duality theorems from constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs).

V-A The Viability Kernel as a Level Set

A common approach to safety is to constrain the system within a known safe set: a set of states which can be made positive invariant through control. The viability kernel 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}} is the largest safe set, and can be recovered from SVFs by simple thresholding under the zeroth-order conditions (11):

Proposition 2 (Thresholding).

Assume VpV_{p} is a safe value function such that the zeroth-order condition (11) holds. Let αinf\alpha_{\mathrm{inf}} and αsup\alpha_{\mathrm{sup}} be the left-hand side and right-hand side of (11), respectively, for the corresponding 𝕋\mathbb{T}. For all α∈(αinf,αsup]\alpha\in(\alpha_{\mathrm{inf}},\alpha_{\mathrm{sup}}], we have:

𝒳V\displaystyle{\mathcal{X}_{V}} ={x,Vp​(x)≥α},\displaystyle=\left\{x,~V_{p}(x)\geq\alpha\right\}, if​𝕋=ℝ+,\displaystyle\text{if}~\mathbb{T}=\mathbb{R}^{+}, (19a)
𝒳V\displaystyle{\mathcal{X}_{V}} ={x,∃u∈𝒬V[x],r(x,u)+γVp(x)≥α},\displaystyle=\left\{x,~\exists u\in{\mathcal{Q}_{V}}[x],r(x,u)+\gamma V_{p}(x)\geq\alpha\right\}, if​𝕋=ℕ,\displaystyle\text{if}~\mathbb{T}=\mathbb{N}\hphantom{{}^{+}}, (19b)

where 𝒬V​[x]⊂𝒰{\mathcal{Q}_{V}}[x]\subset\mathcal{U} is the slice of 𝒬V{\mathcal{Q}_{V}} in state xx and 𝒬V{\mathcal{Q}_{V}} is defined in Theorem 1.

Proof:

This is an immediate consequence of (11). ∎

Remark 4.

The simple expression of 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}} of (19a) also holds in discrete time with further assumptions on the value function. Assume that:

inf𝒳VV>sup𝒳UVp.\inf_{\mathcal{X}_{V}}V>\sup_{{\mathcal{X}_{U}}}V_{p}. (20)

Then, Equation (19a) holds for discrete time as well with the same values of αinf\alpha_{\mathrm{inf}} and αsup\alpha_{\mathrm{sup}} as for continuous time. Note that, under Assumption 1, (20) can always be enforced by further increasing the penalty pp. A sufficient lower value of pp for this to hold can be derived from Lemma 2.

Expressing safe sets as level sets is at the heart of HJ reachability and CBFs. We explore their connections to SVFs.

V-A1 Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability

The goal of HJ reachability is to find the set of states from where the system can be robustly driven into a target set, which is called the backwards-rechable tube of the target set [12]. For example, the backwards-reachable tube of the failure set is the unviability kernel 𝒳U{\mathcal{X}_{U}}. The main method [23, 17] is to cast this as an optimal control problem and find a value function VBRTV_{\mathrm{BRT}} defined similarly as in (5), but where the integral is replaced with an infimum over time:

VBRT:x∈𝒳↦supu∈𝔘inft≥0r⁡(ϕxu​(t)).V_{\mathrm{BRT}}:x\in\mathcal{X}\mapsto\sup_{u\in\mathfrak{U}}~\inf_{t\geq 0}~r(\phi_{x}^{u}(t)). (21)

Here, the function rr is the signed distance to the failure set. Its main difference with the reward used in this article is that VBRTV_{\mathrm{BRT}} does not have an integral structure over a trajectory; in technical terms, VBRTV_{\mathrm{BRT}} is not a Lagrange-type value function [47, Section III.3]. It instead captures the minimum value of rr over the trajectory; VBRT​(x)V_{\mathrm{BRT}}(x) is the closest distance between the trajectory and the failure set. Once this value function is known, the backwards-reachable tube (i.e., the unviability kernel) can be recovered as a level set. It can then be used to solve a classic optimal control problem with safety guarantees, for instance by applying a backup controller when the system is about to exit the viability kernel [13, 17]. Hsu et al. [49] combine this formulation with a task-related reward, and achieve a value function that is both task-optimal and safe, though not a Lagrange-type one.

For clarity of exposition, we have defined SVFs for Lagrange-type value functions only. Nonetheless, they extend to other forms of optimal control by changing the cost functional GG appropriately in (5) and ( C ). A key advantage of the Lagrange cost (3) is its compatibility with classical RL.

V-A2 Control Barrier Functions

To connect SVFs to CBFs, we limit the problem setting to continuous time, 𝕋=ℝ+\mathbb{T}=\mathbb{R}^{+}. For details, including other formulations of CBFs, we recommend the review by Ames et al. [15].

In a nutshell, a CBF of a closed set 𝒞⊂𝒳\mathcal{C}\subset\mathcal{X} is a continuously differentiable function h:𝒟→ℝh:\mathcal{D}\to\mathbb{R}, with 𝒞⊆𝒟\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathcal{D}, such that 𝒞\mathcal{C} is the 00-superlevel set of hh. Additionally, hh must satisfy the following two properties: it increases along trajectories in 𝒟∖𝒞\mathcal{D}\setminus\mathcal{C}, and can locally increase at the boundary of 𝒞\mathcal{C}. This means that for every state at the boundary of 𝒞\mathcal{C}, there exists a control input that makes the derivative of hh along the trajectory nonnegative at this point. For brevity, we will not introduce a formal definition of CBFs and refer to [15, Definition 2]. The following proposition connects SVFs to CBFs:

Proposition 3.

Let VpV_{p} be a safe value function such that the zeroth-order condition (11) holds. Assume that Vp|𝒳VV_{p|{\mathcal{X}_{V}}} is continuously differentiable and 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}} is compact. Also assume that ∂Vp|𝒳V∂x​(x)≠0\frac{\partial V_{p|{\mathcal{X}_{V}}}}{\partial x}(x)\neq 0 for all x∈∂𝒳Vx\in\partial{\mathcal{X}_{V}}, where ∂𝒳V\partial{\mathcal{X}_{V}} is the boundary of 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}}. Then, for all α∈(αinf,αsup]\alpha\in(\alpha_{\mathrm{inf}},\alpha_{\mathrm{sup}}], the function h=Vp|𝒳V−αh=V_{p|{\mathcal{X}_{V}}}-\alpha is a control barrier function of 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}}.

Here, αinf\alpha_{\mathrm{inf}} and αsup\alpha_{\mathrm{sup}} are defined in Proposition 2. This result extends the one presented in [16] for value functions coming from HJ reachability analysis.

Proof:

The fact that 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}} is the 00-superlevel set of hh is immediate from Proposition 2. We use [15, Theorem 3], which states that a differentiable indicator function g:𝒞→ℝg:\mathcal{C}\to\mathbb{R} of a compact set 𝒞\mathcal{C} is a barrier function of this set if i) ∂g∂x​(x)≠0\frac{\partial g}{\partial x}(x)\neq 0 for all xx on ∂𝒞\partial\mathcal{C}; and ii) there exists a control law that renders 𝒞\mathcal{C} invariant. We take 𝒞=𝒳V\mathcal{C}={\mathcal{X}_{V}} and g=hg=h. The first condition is assumed, and the second comes from the definition of 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}}. ∎It is worth noting that CBFs are typically used to enforce positive invariance of a conservative subset of 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}} that is specified a priori, and not the entire viability kernel 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}}. Specifying such a set is often non-trivial, since not all subsets of 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}} can be made positive invariant. Indeed, choosing h=Vp|𝒳V−αh=V_{p|{\mathcal{X}_{V}}}-\alpha for α>αsup\alpha>\alpha_{\mathrm{sup}} may not yield a CBF unless stronger assumptions are made for the the system dynamics and/or reward function [21, 49]. Alternatively to learning a value-function that is also a CBF, a CBF can also be learned from samples of dynamics transitions alone [20, 50]: this is because positive invariance is a property of the system dynamics, and separate from optimality and rewards.

V-B Duality Properties of Constrained Markov Decision Processes

There is a more general set of problems modeled as CMDPs, which deal with maximizing a return while simultaneously constraining a running cost under a given threshold [41]. Our definition of safety is therefore a special case of CMDPs where the running cost is ρ\rho and the threshold is 00; we refer to it as the 00-risk CMDP, as opposed to bounded-risk CMDPs.

We will now demonstrate that our results do not generally extend to probabilistic safety with a non-zero threshold. More specifically, it is not always possible to find a penalty such that all solutions of the penalized problem are both feasible and optimal for the bounded-risk CMDP. This shows that penalties alone are ill-suited to solve RL tasks where a non-zero risk is allowed. The key argument is that solutions to CMDPs are qualitatively different from the ones of MDPs; optimal controllers are stochastic in general [41, Theorem 3.6 , Theorem 3.8]. We illustrate below how this allows the penalized problem to admit solutions that are either unsafe or suboptimal for the bounded-risk CMDP. We also emphasize why strong duality – which is known to hold for CMDPs [41, Theorem 3.6], [51] – is not contradictory with this result. Finally, we pinpoint the special properties of the 00-risk CMDP that make the above concerns void.

The results presented here are reinterpretations of results from [41, Chapter 3] and [51] enabled by our previous results and general duality in optimization [52, Chapter 5]. We restrict ourselves to discrete time and finite state-control sets 𝒳×𝒰\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{U}.

V-B1 Strong Duality does not Guarantee Safety

The bounded-risk CMDP ( C η ) differs from ( C ) in that the risk should only be lower than some threshold η>0\eta>0 in the constraint:

supu∈𝔘𝔼x∼μ⁡[G⁡(x,u)],s.t.ρ(x,u)≤η,∀x∈𝒳V.\begin{split}\sup_{u\in\mathfrak{U}}&\quad\expected_{x\sim\mu}\left[G(x,u)\right],\\ \textrm{s.t.}&\quad\rho(x,u)\leq\eta,\quad\forall x\in{\mathcal{X}_{V}}.\end{split} (𝒞η\mathcal{C}_{\eta})

In contrast, ( C ) is equivalent to ( C η ) with η=0\eta=0. Strong duality is known to hold in general for ( C η ) [41, Theorem 3.6], [51]. Here, strong duality guarantees the existence of a penalty p⋆p^{\star} such that there is at least one controller u⋆∈𝔘u^{\star}\in\mathfrak{U} such that u⋆u^{\star} is feasible and optimal for both the original problem ( C η ) and the penalized problem ( P ) [52, Section 5.5.5]. However, not all solutions of the penalized problem ( P ) satisfy the constraints of ( C η ). In other words, some solutions of the dual11 1 We abuse notation here by not considering the constant term p⋆⋅ηp^{\star}\cdot\eta in the dual problem ( P ), which is harmless as we only consider the argmax\argmax. are not feasible for the primal [52, Section 5.5.5]. The outcome of an RL algorithm is therefore not guaranteed to be safe when η>0\eta>0, even with the optimal penalty p⋆p^{\star}. In fact, primal-dual algorithms for RL typically assume feasibility of the found solutions [53, Assumption 2]. We explain below how optimal but unsafe solutions can arise, based on an example and theoretical results from [41, Chapter 3].

Example 1 (Unsafe Solutions with 00 Duality Gap).

Consider the MDP presented in Figure 1, with γ=0.1\gamma=0.1 and η=0.01\eta=0.01. The corresponding bounded-risk CMDP is:

argmaxu𝔼⁡[G⁡(x1,u)],s.t.𝔼⁡[ρ⁡(x1,u)]≤η,\begin{split}\argmax_{u}~&\expected\left[G(x_{1},u)\right],\\ \textrm{s.t.}~&\expected\left[\rho(x_{1},u)\right]\leq\eta,\end{split} (22)

where the controller is allowed to be stochastic, thus requiring expected values. This problem boils down to finding the optimal probability θ⋆\theta^{\star} that should be assigned to the control input u2u_{2}:

argmaxθ∈[0,1]γ⋅θ,s.t.γ⋅θ≤η,\begin{split}\argmax_{\theta\in[0,1]}~&\gamma\cdot\theta,\\ \textrm{s.t.}~&\gamma\cdot\theta\leq\eta,\end{split} (23)

which has solution θ⋆=0.1\theta^{\star}=0.1. Now, consider the penalized problem, with p∈ℝ+p\in\mathbb{R}^{+}:

argmaxθ∈[0,1]γ⋅θ⋅(1−γ⋅p).\argmax_{\theta\in[0,1]}~\gamma\cdot\theta\cdot(1-\gamma\cdot p). (24)

Strong duality holds with penalty p=p⋆=10p=p^{\star}=10, such that (1−γ​p)=0(1-\gamma p)=0; this is the only penalty for which θ⋆=0.1\theta^{\star}=0.1 also maximizes (24). However, we trivially see that any θ∈[0,1]\theta\in[0,1] has the same objective value for (24).

We observe the following:

  1. (i)

    The set of optimal policies of (24) does not depend on η\eta as long as η>0\eta>0;

  2. (ii)

    Not all solutions of the penalized problem (24) are solutions of the bounded-risk problem (22); other solutions are either suboptimal or infeasible;

  3. (iii)

    The solution of (22) is stochastic.

Example 1 illustrates the reasons why simply penalizing failure to solve bounded-risk CMDPs may be problematic. In general, solutions of bounded-risk CMDPs are stochastic, contrary to unconstrained MDPs [41, Theorems 3.6 and 3.8]. Intuitively, this stochasticity enables a tradeoff between visiting high-cost and high-reward regions (𝒳F{\mathcal{X}_{F}} in Example 1) and low-cost but low-reward ones (𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}} in Example 1). Unconstrained MDPs can only yield such stochastic controllers when multiple control inputs in a given state have the same value [44, Chapter 3]. Therefore, the optimal penalty p⋆p^{\star} is the one that makes the values of safe control inputs equal to the ones of unsafe control inputs; in Example 1, controls u1u_{1} and u2u_{2} both have value 00 for p=p⋆p=p^{\star}. Consequently, the optimal return does not depend on how optimal controllers choose between such control inputs, and the whole spectrum between being overly conservative and always failing is allowed. This shows that some solutions of the penalized problem are suboptimal for the bounded-risk problem, and that others can be infeasible. For this reason, strong duality alone guarantees neither safety nor optimality of the solutions of the penalized problem when η>0\eta>0. In that sense, our result is stronger than strong duality, as we explain in the next section.

V-B2 An Unconstrained MDP in the Viability Kernel

The above analysis stresses the special and beneficial properties of the 00-risk problem ( C ). It is fundamentally different from general bounded-risk CMDPs ( C η ), with η>0\eta>0. In a nutshell, the 00-risk problem reduces to an unconstrained MDP inside of 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}}.

The constraint in ( C ) exhibits a very specific property compared to other bounded-risk constraints, in that it can be directly translated as a constraint on trajectories. Namely, trajectories should be confined in the viability kernel 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}}. Therefore, the constrained problem ( C ) can be reformulated as an unconstrained problem with state space 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}} and state-dependent control space 𝒰​(x)=𝒬V​[x]\mathcal{U}(x)={\mathcal{Q}_{V}}[x]. This interpretation makes very clear why penalization is effective in this case: high enough penalties give low enough values to states in 𝒳U{\mathcal{X}_{U}}, such that optimal controllers are deterministic and stay in 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}}.

Remark 5.

Since the 00-risk problem is essentially an unconstrained MDP in 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}}, it has deterministic optimal controllers. Its optimal controllers also do not depend on the initial state distribution μ\mu. This justifies a posteriori the fact that we can restrict ourselves to deterministic controllers to solve ( C ) without loss of generality and why μ\mu does not play a role in our results. These properties are not true for general CMDPs [41, Chapter 3]; this is why we allowed stochastic controllers in Example 1.

VI Safe Value Functions and Designing Reward Functions

The structure revealed in Equations (11) and (18) provide important guidelines not just for choosing p⋆p^{\star} and α\alpha, but for the general problem of designing a reward function. We first solve a continuous-time example analytically to highlight the relationship of discount rate, time-to-failure, and penalties. Then we present a discretized example to illustrate how various forms of reward shaping affect the minimum penalty and thresholds. The code to reproduce these (and more) examples is publicly available22 2 https://github.com/sheim/vibly/tree/TAC22/demos/TAC22.

VI-A Continuous-time Example

To illustrate the influence of the penalty on the value function, we solve the penalized problem analytically on a simple continuous-time example. We consider the following piecewise-affine system:

x˙​(t)={−LTf,if​x∈(−L,0),u⁡(x⁡(t)),if​x∈[0,L),0,otherwise,\dot{x}(t)=\begin{cases}-\frac{L}{{T_{f}}},&\text{if}~x\in(-L,0),\\ u(x(t)),&\text{if}~x\in[0,L),\\ 0,&\text{otherwise,}\end{cases} (25)

with state space 𝒳=[−L,L]\mathcal{X}=[-L,L] and finite control space 𝒰={−v,0,v}\mathcal{U}=\{-v,0,v\}, where LL and vv are positive constants. We define failure with 𝒳F={−L}{\mathcal{X}_{F}}=\{-L\}; the trajectory immediately stops when it enters 𝒳F{\mathcal{X}_{F}}. This results in the viability kernel 𝒳V=[0,L]{\mathcal{X}_{V}}=[0,L] and unviability kernel 𝒳U=(−L,0){\mathcal{X}_{U}}=(-L,0). It is straightforward to verify that Assumption 1 holds with constant Tf{T_{f}}. Intuitively, this model can be thought of as a robot driving on a shelf of size [0,L][0,L]; the robot can move forward or backward at constant speed ±v\pm v. If, however, the robot crosses the ledge of the shelf at x=0x=0, it falls at constant speed L/Tf{L}/{{T_{f}}} until it reaches the ground at x=−Lx=-L and breaks.

We use the following reward function:

r⁡(x)={−1,if​x∈[0,L),1,if​x∈(−L,0),0,if​x∈{−L,L}.r(x)=\begin{cases}-1,&\text{if}~x\in[0,L),\\ 1,&\text{if}~x\in(-L,0),\\ 0,&\text{if}~x\in\{-L,L\}.\end{cases} (26)

This reward leads the agent to failure from some viable states. We therefore also penalize failure with the penalty pp; the total reward is r−p⋅δ𝒳Fr-p\cdot\delta_{{\mathcal{X}_{F}}}. We illustrate with this example how a choice of p>p⋆p>p^{\star} yields an SVF and how p⋆p^{\star}, τ\tau, and Tf{T_{f}} interact.

VI-A1 Scaling the Penalty

The optimal control consists in either going to and remaining at x=Lx=L, or falling from the shelf. From this observation we deduce the value function for x∈𝒳Vx\in{\mathcal{X}_{V}}:

Vp​(x)=max{τ[ex−Lv⋅τ−1],τ⁡[(2−e−Tfτ)⋅e−xv⋅τ−1]−p⋅e−Tf+xvτ}.\begin{split}V_{p}(x)=\max~&\left\{\tau\left[\vphantom{e^{-\frac{{T_{f}}}{\tau}}}e^{\frac{x-L}{v\cdot\tau}}-1\right],\right.\\ &\left.~~\tau\left[\left(2-e^{-\frac{{T_{f}}}{\tau}}\right)\cdot e^{-\frac{x}{v\cdot\tau}}-1\right]\right.\\ &\left.\qquad-p\cdot e^{-\frac{{T_{f}}+\frac{x}{v}}{\tau}}\right\}.\end{split} (27)

In contrast, in 𝒳U{\mathcal{X}_{U}}, the trajectory goes to failure at speed LTf\frac{L}{{T_{f}}}; we get the following expression for x∈𝒳Ux\in{\mathcal{X}_{U}}:

Vp​(x)=τ⁡[1−e−Tfτ​(1+xL)]−p⋅e−Tfτ​(1+xL).V_{p}(x)=\tau\left[1-e^{-\frac{{T_{f}}}{\tau}\left(1+\frac{x}{L}\right)}\right]-p\cdot e^{-\frac{{T_{f}}}{\tau}\left(1+\frac{x}{L}\right)}. (28)

The agent thus remains in 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}} for all time if, and only if, the max\max in (27) is equal to its first argument in x=0x=0. This yields the minimum value for pp for an SVF:

p>τ⁡[2−e−Lv⋅τ]⋅eTfτ−τ​=˙​p⋆.p>\tau\left[2-e^{-\frac{L}{v\cdot\tau}}\right]\cdot e^{\frac{{T_{f}}}{\tau}}-\tau~\dot{=}~p^{\star}. (29)

The RHS is equal to p⋆p^{\star} as defined in (18a); we recover Theorem 2 without directly using it.

As pp passes p⋆p^{\star}, values in 𝒳U{\mathcal{X}_{U}} keep decreasing and the difference between the thresholds αinf\alpha_{\mathrm{inf}} and αsup\alpha_{\mathrm{sup}} increases (Fig. 2, top). The viability kernel can easily be recovered via thresholding thanks to the discontinuity in x=0x=0. Nevertheless, the value α=0\alpha=0 is not a suitable threshold; this is due to the negative values of the reward in 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}}. We further illustrate this in Section VI-E.

VI-A2 Discount Rate, Time-to-Failure, and Penalties

While Equation (18) is in general only an upper-bound, it is tight on this example; p⋆p^{\star} is the lowest penalty such that VpV_{p} is safe for p>p⋆p>p^{\star}. This emphasizes the role of the discount rate τ\tau and time-to-failure Tf{T_{f}} on the minimum penalty (Fig. 2, middle and bottom). A large Tf{T_{f}} can lead to a large penalty due to the exponential dependency p⋆∝eTf/τp^{\star}\propto e^{{{T_{f}}}/{\tau}}. A higher discount rate may help mitigate that problem; it more easily propagates the penalty signal up a failed trajectory. However, the discount rate is also a crucial parameter determining the safe, optimal behavior. In fact, if the reward function can be negative inside 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}}, a large τ\tau can actually lower inf𝒳VV\inf_{\mathcal{X}_{V}}V (the RHS of (11)), increase p⋆p^{\star}, and thus encourage failure.

A suitable choice of τ\tau needs to consider both of these independent criteria, even if the time-to-failure Tf{T_{f}} is the main driver of this choice. A long Tf{T_{f}} essentially indicates that there exist controllers that can delay an inevitable failure. While it may seem unintuitive that the existence of such controllers increases the relative gravity of failure, it adds a new interpretation to the benefit of “fail fast”. We may conclude that if there are two causally related unviable states, it is advantageous to penalize the one that occurs first.

VI-B Numerical Example

To illustrate the influence of the reward on the value function, we use a simple two dimensional system for which we can numerically compute and visualize both the viability kernel and value functions. The system dynamics are

x˙1=x2,x˙2=−gx12+ω2​x1+u,\begin{split}\dot{x}_{1}&=x_{2},\\ \dot{x}_{2}&=-\frac{g}{x_{1}^{2}}+\omega^{2}x_{1}+u,\end{split} (30)

with state x=(x1,x2)∈[0,16]×[−5,7]x=\left(x_{1},x_{2}\right)\in\left[0,16\right]\times\left[-5,7\right], control input u∈[−1,1]u\in\left[-1,1\right], and system parameters g=10g=10 and ω=0.1\omega=0.1. The dynamics can be loosely interpreted as a satellite orbiting at constant angular velocity ω\omega, with g/x12{g}/{x_{1}^{2}} the gravitational force, ω2​x1\omega^{2}x_{1} the centripetal force, and uu a radial thruster. To keep the computation time of value functions low, we discretize the system in space with a 401×301 grid over the states, and discretize in time by applying the control input uu with a zero-order-hold for a period of 1 second, and integrating the continuous time dynamics. This allows us to explore different combinations of penalties, rewards, and discount factors, and easily visualize the results.

The failure set is 𝒳F={x:x1≤1​ or ​x1≥15}{\mathcal{X}_{F}}=\{x:x_{1}\leq 1\text{ or }x_{1}\geq 15\}, representing the satellite crashing or moving beyond radio communication range. The continuous-time dynamics (30) don’t satisfy Assumption 1; nevertheless, the discretized system trivially satisfies it since its state-control space is finite.

All value functions in the following are computed by brute force using value iteration [54, Chapter 7.3], with a discount factor γ=0.6\gamma=0.6, and p⋆p^{\star} is rounded off to integer values.

VI-C Success and Failure are Conceptually Independent

Intuition tells us that success implies avoiding failure, yet avoiding failure does not imply success. This intuition becomes clear when a task is translated into a parsimonious reward function. Arguably, the most parsimonious reward describing a task is to simply assign a positive reward for states associated with task success, and zero reward everywhere else. The definition of a failure set implies that task success should only involve states inside the viability kernel 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}}; the value function for such a reward function is naturally zero outside 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}}, and at least zero inside. In fact, the value inside 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}} is zero only for states from which the task cannot be successfully completed. We thus see that task success and failure are separate concepts: although the value function (and optimal controller) of a parsimonious reward is automatically safe whenever the task can be successfully completed, it does not enforce the strict inequality condition in (11). At the same time, the penalty has no effect on values in 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}}, and the value function is made safe by any penalty greater than zero.

Consider as desired task for our satellite model to reach the equilibrium point at x=(10,0)x=\left(10,0\right). A parsimonious reward function is to return one at equilibrium and zero everywhere else. An SVF for the parsimonious reward function, with penalty p=1p=1 assigned to the failure set 𝒳F={x:x1≤1​ or ​x1≥15}{\mathcal{X}_{F}}=\{x:x_{1}\leq 1\text{ or }x_{1}\geq 15\}, is shown in Fig. 3.

Note that for this system, a penalty is not strictly necessary to enforce safety, since the equilibrium point can be reached from any state x∈𝒳Vx\in{\mathcal{X}_{V}}.

VI-D Recovering the Viability Kernel

The independence of success and failure suggests that we can consider safety independently from any specific task; this property provides the simplest parameters for recovering the viability kernel. The degenerate reward function r⁡(x,u)=0r(x,u)=0 does not require even estimates of 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}} to design. It can be immediately seen in Equation (18) that all terms in p⋆p^{\star} go to zero, and any non-zero penalty will induce an SVF. We see from the RHS of Equation (11) that αsup\alpha_{\mathrm{sup}} is also zero, and thus 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}} can be recovered by thresholding VpV_{p} with α=0\alpha=0, as shown in Fig. 4.

VI-E Reward Shaping Guidelines

Parsimonious reward functions are rarely used in practice: they are typically too sparse, and it may not be known how to describe task success mathematically. It is common to design a surrogate reward that is denser, or has a smooth structure more amenable to optimization. This practice is called reward shaping. It is when this surrogate reward function is poorly specified that penalties become critical.

We distinguish three categories of modifications, based on whether the reward is positive or negative, and lies inside or outside 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}}, and examine their effect on p⋆p^{\star} and α\alpha. Although 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}} is typically unknown a priori, over- and under-approximations are sometimes known from domain knowledge [55], and for certain classes of systems, they can be estimated [50, 56, 57].

VI-E1 Benign Rewards

Adding positive rewards to states in 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}} and/or negative rewards in 𝒳∖𝒳V\mathcal{X}\setminus{\mathcal{X}_{V}} does not increase p⋆p^{\star} and can, in fact, potentially decrease it. Such modifications can only increase the RHS and decrease the left-hand side (LHS) of Equation (11), and thus relaxes the condition for SVFs.

If only benign rewards are used to describe a task, the resulting value function may no longer be optimal compared to a parsimonious reward function, but it remains safe and easy to specify: we have p⋆=0p^{\star}=0 and α=0\alpha=0. When combined with other types of rewards, benign rewards reduce p⋆p^{\star}.

VI-E2 Positive Rewards Outside 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}}

Assigning positive rewards outside 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}} can increase R𝒬U{R}_{{\mathcal{Q}_{U}}}, which we see in Equation (18) increases the minimum penalty p⋆p^{\star}. We illustrate this effect with a surrogate reward function that encourages the satellite to remain within a threshold of the equilibrium position, without considering its velocity (Fig. 5 top):

r⁡(x,u)={1if,|x1−10|≤10otherwise.r(x,u)=\begin{cases}1&\text{if},|x_{1}-10|\leq 1\\ 0&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (31)

Although the peak of the value function remains centered around the equilibrium point, a relatively high penalty of p=111p=111 is needed to recover an SVF (Fig. 5 bottom).

Positive rewards outside 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}} can also increase the LHS of Equation (11), and consequently αinf\alpha_{\mathrm{inf}} in Equation (19), making the choice of a thresholding value α\alpha more difficult. Nonetheless, if only positive rewards are used, αsup\alpha_{\mathrm{sup}} must be non-negative. There is then always a p>p⋆p>p^{\star} such that the threshold α=0\alpha=0 recovers the viability kernel from an SVF.

VI-E3 Negative Rewards inside 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}}

Assigning negative rewards inside 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}} can decrease inf𝒳VV\inf_{{\mathcal{X}_{V}}}V and R𝒬V{R}_{{\mathcal{Q}_{V}}}, which again leads to a higher minimum penalty p⋆p^{\star}. We illustrate this effect with a surrogate reward function that discourages the satellite from high velocities, without considering its position, together with a quadratic cost on the control input (Fig. 6 top):

r⁡(x,u)={−1−u2if,|x2|≥2−u2otherwise.r(x,u)=\begin{cases}-1-u^{2}&\text{if},|x_{2}|\geq 2\\ -u^{2}&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (32)

Again, the peak of the value function remains centered correctly; however, there are regions of the viability kernel 𝒳V{\mathcal{X}_{V}} that have a lower value than regions outside, until the penalty is increased to at least p=136p=136 (Fig. 6 bottom).

Furthermore, negative rewards can influence both the RHS and LHS of (11), making it substantially more difficult to choose a thresholding value α\alpha.

VII Discussion and Outlook

We have identified how rewards can preserve viability through the necessary structure of an SVF: a value function that is both optimal with respect to a given task, and safely avoids a given failure set. We then provide the zeroth-order sufficient condition for safety, which builds on the intuition that unsafe states should be suboptimal. Furthermore, we have shown under mild assumptions that the SVF structure can always be enforced by simply shaping the reward function with any sufficiently large penalty on the failure set. We show how the upper bound for the minimum penalty depends on the reward, discount rate, and system dynamics, and provide an explicit formula (cf.  (18)) to compute it. Although the inputs to this formula are often difficult to obtain in practice, they provide insight into the problem, and we discuss several theory-backed heuristics for designing an appropriate reward function. We expect the insight developed in this article will allow engineers to design reward functions more effectively, while also offering better interpretability of penalty terms.

The new notion of safe value function has many connections to existing tools for safe control, such as Hamilton-Jacobi reachability and control barrier functions. We examine when these objects are equivalent and when they differ. Since important objects like the viability kernel can easily be recovered, safe value functions do not lose the advantages of considering safety constraints as separate objects. We have also shown that penalizing failure is not suited to deal with general bounded-risk constraints. This result suggests that it is neither necessary nor easier to resort to more elaborate definitions of safety when the dynamics has controllable invariant sets.

The zeroth-order condition we provide is only a sufficient condition, and only applies to systems with discontinuous value functions. An exciting open question is to derive higher-order conditions for safety of continuous value functions. This would open the way to other classes of reward shaping for which safety can be checked a priori and thus, facilitate the design of rewards for multiple criteria.

We have restricted our attention to deterministic dynamics. Many practical applications account for uncertainty in the model in the form of process noise or exogenous disturbances. We expect our results to extend to this setting by considering the notion of invariance kernel [4, Definition 2.9.2], sometimes called the discriminating kernel [13], a robust extension of the viability kernel. When this invariance kernel is empty, our definition of safety is not suited to describe the system, and one should consider an alternative such as bounded risk constraints. In this case, we expect that penalizing failures actually harms the optimality of penalized-optimal controllers.

Our long-term goal is to learn provably safe, optimal controllers for the constrained problem. In practice, value functions and controllers are parameterized to allow for efficient representations in high dimensions, e.g., with deep neural networks. The previous analysis breaks down in this case, as the optimal dynamic programming identity is no longer satisfied and values inside and outside the viability kernel are no longer independent. Whether a finite penalty ensures safety and constrained-optimality of penalized-optimal, parameterized controllers then remains an important open question.

eTτ⋅(G−p​ρ)​(x)\displaystyle e^{\frac{T}{\tau}}\cdot(G-p\rho)(x) ≤sup𝒳∖𝒳VVp+I0,\displaystyle\leq\sup_{\mathcal{X}\setminus{\mathcal{X}_{V}}}V_{p}+I_{0}, (44)

where we used the fact δ​t=0{\delta t}=0. When 𝕋=ℕ\mathbb{T}=\mathbb{N}, we have instead δ​t=1{\delta t}=1 and use the counting measure for integration, which yields:

eT+1τ⋅V⁡(x)\displaystyle e^{\frac{T+1}{\tau}}\cdot V(x) ≥inf𝒳VV+I0+e1τ⋅R𝒬V,\displaystyle\geq\inf_{{\mathcal{X}_{V}}}V+I_{0}+e^{\frac{1}{\tau}}\cdot{R}_{{\mathcal{Q}_{V}}}, (45)
eT+1τ⋅(G−p​ρ)​(x)\displaystyle e^{\frac{T+1}{\tau}}\cdot(G-p\rho)(x) ≤sup𝒳∖𝒳VVp+I0+e1τ⋅R𝒬U.\displaystyle\leq\sup_{\mathcal{X}\setminus{\mathcal{X}_{V}}}V_{p}+I_{0}+e^{\frac{1}{\tau}}\cdot{R}_{{\mathcal{Q}_{U}}}. (46)

For completeness, we should now discuss the case when y=ϕxuF​(T+δ​t)y=\phi_{x}^{u_{F}}(T+{\delta t}) is in 𝒳F{\mathcal{X}_{F}}; i.e., when an ϵ¯\bar{\epsilon} cannot be chosen as described after (36). The previous computations still hold by simply writing the dynamic programming equations until time TT instead of T+ϵT+\epsilon, and defining the controller uu with some ϵ∈𝕋\epsilon\in\mathbb{T} small enough. Therefore, Equations (43)–(46) hold in this case as well.

Since the zeroth-order condition (11) holds, these inequalities imply that

eT+δ​tτ​V​(x)>eT+δ​tτ⋅(G−p⋅ρ)​(x,uF).e^{\frac{T+{\delta t}}{\tau}}\,V(x)>e^{\frac{T+{\delta t}}{\tau}}\cdot(G-p\cdot\rho)(x,u_{F}). (47)

As this holds for all x∈𝒳Vx\in{\mathcal{X}_{V}} and uF∈𝔘∖𝔘safe​(x)u_{F}\in\mathfrak{U}\setminus\mathfrak{U}_{\mathrm{safe}}(x), this shows that (ii) in Lemma 3 is satisfied. ∎

-B Finite Time-to-Failure and Lipschitz are conflicting yet useful models

Assumption 1 (the maximum time-to-failure is uniformly upper-bounded) directly conflicts with the Lipschitz-continuity assumption, which is commonly used to model many systems of general interest. We reconcile this conflict with the observation that these assumptions are useful for separate purposes: Assumption 1 more closely matches empirical observations when dealing with safety, even when a Lipschitz dynamics model is useful for the purpose of control or prediction.

We provide two examples, from the field of legged robotics and from experimental observations of animal motion.

-B1 Linear inverted pendulum model of walking

A linear inverted pendulum model is commonly used to control foot-step locations of bipedal robots [58, 59, 55]. For this model, the relevant dynamics become linear, and it is possible to solve in closed form for the so-called N-step capture region [59]: the set of foot-step locations from which it is possible to return to a stand-still in NN steps. The formula for the maximum footstep location (which is the border of the capture region) dNd_{N} reads [59, Eq. 16, rewritten for clarity]:

dN=ℓm​a​x​∑i=1N(e−Δ​ts′)i,d_{N}=\ell_{max}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(e^{-\Delta t_{s}^{\prime}})^{i}, (48)

where ℓm​a​x\ell_{max} is the maximum step-length, and Δ​ts′\Delta t_{s}^{\prime} is the minimum step-time (time required to swing the foot to the new location). If we take NN to infinity, the border of the inifinite-step capture region is

d∞=ℓm​a​x​e−Δ​ts′1−e−Δ​ts′,d_{\infty}=\ell_{max}\frac{e^{-\Delta t_{s}^{\prime}}}{1-e^{-\Delta t_{s}^{\prime}}}, (49)

and is closed. Note that, as can be seen in [59, Fig. 1], the viability kernel is a strict superset of the infinite-step capture region, implying there are states in which it is possible to avoid ever falling down, but also impossible to stop walking. This model also implies that there are states from which it takes infinitely many steps to slow down, and conversely infinitely many steps to fall, even though falling may be unavoidable. Personal experience tells us this is not true. In fact, numerical computations for the same and similar models show that if failure can be avoided, it is always possible to come to a stop in just two steps [55, 60, 46]. Practice tells us this is true for real robots as well, and experimental observation suggests it is also true for human walking [61]. In other words, this model and its capture regions are very useful for the purposes of control, even though they do not match with real observations on the border ∂𝒳V\partial{\mathcal{X}_{V}}. This is not a problem because the model’s accuracy at the border is not important for control; it does become important to estimate time to failure, as in our setting.

-B2 Landing Trajectory of Honeybees

Our second example is the one developed in [62], which studies the time-to-touchdown of honeybees during landing. The authors find that bees essentially follow an exponential trajectory at landing, which implies a theoretically infinite time-to-touchdown. This is explicitly written by the authors [62, after Eq. 11]:

“Thus, the projected time to touchdown does not decrease linearly with time, as it would if the bee approached the surface at constant speed. Neither does the bee decelerate abruptly when the projected time to touchdown falls below a critical value, as flies seem to do before landing on a small target. Rather, the landing bee decelerates continuously, and in such a way as to maintain a constant projected time to touchdown. This, in effect, is the reason why touchdown theoretically requires infinite time.”

Nevertheless, bees can land. The authors give the following explanation [62, after Eq. 4]:

“This, however, is not a problem in reality because extension of the legs prior to landing ensures that touchdown usually occurs at a nonzero height above the ground.”

Again, a reasonable model to describe the trajectory of bees yields unrealistic predictions of the “time-to-reach”.
